analysis_steps.goal: Create Stokes I, Q, U mosaics and debiased linear polarization and magnetic field angle maps

method.value: Combine three pointings for MM1-Main and two pointings for MM1-SW using CASA tclean in mosaic mode; compute linear polarization P, debias using Hull & Plambeck (2015) for <=5 sigma_P and sqrt(Q^2 + U^2 - sigma_P^2) for >5 sigma_P; compute polarization angle chi = 0.5 arctan(U/Q) and rotate by 90 deg to get B_POS orientation above 3 sigma_P.

evidence.quote: We combined three and two pointings toward MM1-Main and MM1-SW to clean and image the different stokes parameters in mosaic mode, using the tclean procedure from CASA 5.1.2 (cite: McMullin2007).

The polarization angle maps are derived following $\vcenter{\hbox{$\chi$}} = 0.5\,\mathrm{arctan}\left(U/Q\right)$.

evidence.quote: We computed the velocity that would need to be subtracted in order to bring them back to a state of gravitational equilibrium (i.e., $\alpha_{\mathrm{vir,B}} = 1$).

evidence.loc: Limitations of current observational estimates of the non-thermal supports
evidence.quote: The resulting velocities range from 1.0 to 3.1 $\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, depending on the core.

findings_qualitative.value: Thermal motions (0.06 to 0.14 km s^-1) contribute only marginally to total core linewidths and are dynamically negligible compared to non-thermal motions.

evidence.quote: Thermal motions therefore contribute only marginally to the total linewidths, and are dynamically negligible.

findings_qualitative.value: Moment-1 maps at the three-beam scale systematically reveal coherent velocity gradients and organized structures across the masks, violating the DCF assumption of purely isotropic turbulence.

evidence.loc: Velocity structures in the three-beam area
evidence.quote: The moment-1 maps clearly reveal organized velocity structures and gradients across the three-beam masks, which indicate that large-scale motions add to micro-turbulence to widen the line width.

findings_qualitative.value: In the most massive cores (> 20 M_sun), kinetic support dominates over magnetic support (M_kin/M_phi > 1), opposite to trends found when assuming a uniform velocity dispersion across all cores.

evidence.loc: Magnetic support and its relative contribution
evidence.quote: However, for the most massive objects (five cores above $20\,M_\odot$, one prestellar and four protostellar), turbulence appears to provide a more significant support than magnetic fields. This trend is opposite to that reported by (cite: Cortes2019).

findings_qualitative.value: Both velocity dispersions and magnetic field strengths in W43-MM1 cores are substantially higher than in low-mass star-forming regions, showing that massive protoclusters operate in a different dynamical and magnetic regime.

evidence.loc: Comparison with low-mass studies and models
evidence.quote: Our results therefore emphasize that massive star-forming environments operate in a qualitatively different dynamical regime mimicking a different turbulent regime from their low-mass counterparts.

evidence.loc: Comparison with low-mass studies and models
evidence.quote: Like for motions, this emphasizes the different magnetic regimes operating in low- and high-mass star-forming environments.

claims.hypothesis: Core-scale kinetic and magnetic support can be reliably quantified using molecular linewidths, DCF polarization analysis, and the volume-only virial theorem.
claims.experiment: Measured core-scale velocity dispersions for 45 cores (DCN, 13CS, CH3CN) and extrapolated DCF magnetic field strengths for 21 cores to compute alpha_kin, lambda_B, and alpha_vir,B.
claims.result: 16 of 24 cores with turbulence alone (~70%) have alpha_kin > 1, and 18 of 21 cores with both estimates (~85%, including 11 protostellar cores) have alpha_vir,B > 1 (16 with alpha_vir,B > 2).
claims.finding: Simplified volume-only virial analysis and raw linewidth measurements systematically overestimate non-thermal support in cores because of contamination by organized motions (1-3 km s^-1 infall/converging flows) and the omission of virial surface terms.

evidence.quote: Combining both estimates, 18 cores ($\sim 85\,\%$) are found with $\alpha_{\mathrm{vir,B}} > 1$. These numbers are unexpectedly high, especially for protostellar cores that are expected to be undergoing collapse.

We conclude that the contamination of the measured linewidths by organized motions (of order 1-3 $\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ and consistent with previous observational studies), together with the omission of surface terms in the observational virial theorem, prevents us from accurately measuring the non-thermal support in cores.

claims.hypothesis: Using individual core velocity dispersions and temperatures alters the inferred scaling of virial support and magnetic vs. kinetic dominance with core mass compared to assuming a uniform velocity dispersion.
claims.experiment: Computed M_kin/M_phi and alpha_vir,B using individual core linewidths and temperatures, and compared with Appendix 10 where a single median velocity dispersion is applied to all cores.
claims.result: With individual velocity dispersions, no anti-correlation between alpha_vir,B and core mass is found, and all five cores above 20 M_sun have M_kin/M_phi > 1; using a single median velocity dispersion artificially recovers the anti-correlation where massive cores appear gravitationally dominated.
claims.finding: Adopting core-specific velocity dispersions is essential for virial analyses and shows that kinetic motions dominate over magnetic support in the most massive cores (> 20 M_sun).

evidence.loc: Magnetic support and its relative contribution
evidence.quote: However, for the most massive objects (five cores above $20\,M_\odot$, one prestellar and four protostellar), turbulence appears to provide a more significant support than magnetic fields. This trend is opposite to that reported by (cite: Cortes2019).

evidence.loc: Impact of a common velocity dispersion on core support
evidence.quote: In this configuration, we recover the usual trend reported in studies (cite: Cortes2016; Cortes2019) that rely on a single, global velocity dispersion: the most massive cores appear gravitationally dominated with an anti-correlation between the level of support and the mass of the cores.

claims.hypothesis: The high-mass prestellar cores in W43-MM1 (#17, #134, #136) are supported against gravitational collapse by non-thermal (turbulent + magnetic) pressure.
claims.experiment: Computed total virial parameter alpha_vir,B and kinetic-to-magnetic support ratio M_kin/M_phi for cores #17, #134, and #136.
claims.result: alpha_vir,B is 2.19 (core #17), 3.12 (core #134), and 11.84 (core #136); cores #17 and #136 have M_kin/M_phi < 1 (0.36 and 0.62, B_core > 30 mG), whereas core #134 has M_kin/M_phi = 3.78 (B_core = 12.1 mG); core #6 (no B measurement) has alpha_kin = 0.32 (or 0.55 in text).
claims.finding: High-mass prestellar cores in W43-MM1 appear sufficiently supported when combining turbulent and magnetic support, though small statistics and virial uncertainties prevent establishing whether turbulence or magnetic fields universally dominate.

evidence.loc: Virial equilibrium in the cores of W43-MM1
evidence.quote: The total virial parameter $\alpha_{\mathrm{vir,B}}$ reaches values of about two and three for cores #17 and #134, respectively, while it exceeds ten for core #136.

The high-mass prestellar cores in W43-MM1 appear to be sufficiently supported when both turbulent and magnetic contributions are considered; however, dominant support between turbulence and magnetic fields in the high-mass prestellar phase could not be firmly established with the present data.

why_this_data.value: W43-MM1 is a young, massive, highly dynamical mini-starburst protocluster with high polarization fractions (~5%), a well-characterized core catalog from ALMA-IMF, and dense gas tracers (DCN, 13CS) that reliably peak on cores.

evidence.quote: In the high-mass star-forming regime, the W43-MM1 massive protocluster is an excellent target to investigate the influence of non-thermal support in cores.

We note that we did not identify any superior tracers that more reliably peak on and trace the cores. (cite: Mininni2025) also showed that DCN is one of the molecular lines that best matches the dust emission toward cores.

why_this_method.value: On-Off spectral extraction isolates core emission from environmental gas; the three-beam area (~2.3'') encompasses 10 independent beams to keep DCF angle dispersion uncertainty within 15%; classical DCF with Q=0.5 avoids circularity with Mach-number-dependent Q; Whitworth et al. (2025) Zeeman scaling extrapolates B_POS to core scale.

evidence.quote: We used the same On–Off method as described in (cite: Valeille-Manet2025) (see their Sect. 3.1), which allows to isolate the emission of the cores by subtracting the contribution of their local environment.

To ensure a statistically meaningful estimate of the angular dispersion within each core, we computed it over an area that encompasses 10 beam-independent points. It assures a dispersion value within 15 % from the true dispersion (cite: Cortes2019).

However, since estimating the Alfvénic Mach number itself requires an assumed value of $Q$, adopting a Mach-number-dependent $Q$ would introduce circularity into our analysis. We therefore opted to keep $Q=0.5$, consistent with the value adopted in much of the literature.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Searching N2D+(3-2) and HC3N(24-23) lines for the 11 cores without DCN or 13CS detections (rejected due to non-detection).

evidence.quote: We also searched for emission in the $\mathrm{N_2D^+}$ (3–2) and $\mathrm{HC_3N}$ (24–23) transitions, other efficient tracers of dense gas available in the ALMA-IMF dataset, but without success.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Alternative On-Off annulus configurations (1.5-2.5, 2.0-4.0, 3.5-4.5, and 4.5-5.5 core sizes) tested on five cores; retained 2.5-3.5 for consistency with Valeille-Manet et al. (2025) as differences were <= 0.17 km s^-1.

evidence.quote: We considered four additional configurations (1.5–2.5, 2.0–4.0, 3.5–4.5, and 4.5–5.5 core sizes) and applied them to five cores with existing DCN On-Off measurements (#2, #7, #11, #14, and #15).

The choice of annulus size therefore has no significant impact on the derived linewidths, and we retained the 2.5–3.5 configuration for consistency with the approach adopted in (cite: Valeille-Manet2025).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Adopting a Mach-number-dependent DCF factor Q (Skalidis et al. 2021) or the compressible DCF formulation of Skalidis & Tassis (2021) (gives B_POS ~20% smaller; classical DCF with Q=0.5 retained).

evidence.quote: However, since estimating the Alfvénic Mach number itself requires an assumed value of $Q$, adopting a Mach-number-dependent $Q$ would introduce circularity into our analysis. We therefore opted to keep $Q=0.5$, consistent with the value adopted in much of the literature.

We also compared our results with the method of (cite: Skalidis_Tassis2021), which proposes to replace $Q/\sigma_\theta$ by $1/\sqrt{2\sigma_\theta}$ in the DCF formula to account for non-Alfvénic compressible modes.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Estimating three-beam velocity dispersion from the mean of the second moment map following Polychronakis et al. (2025) (yielded ~20% larger values; Gaussian fit with moment-1 std subtraction retained).

evidence.loc: Velocity structures in the three-beam area
evidence.quote: We also compared our three-beam scale velocity dispersion estimates with the method proposed by (cite: Polychronakis2025), which consists in taking the mean of the second moment map within the three-beam mask of each core as a proxy for the velocity dispersion used in magnetic field estimates.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Ideal MHD flux-freezing extrapolation B proportional to n^(2/3) (Mestel 1966) instead of B proportional to n^0.53 (rejected because n^(2/3) only holds for spherical collapse without dynamically important B or resistive effects).

evidence.quote: However, as shown by (cite: Tritsis2015), the relation $B \,\propto\, n^{2/3}$ is only valid in the case of spherical collapse, which is not expected when magnetic fields are dynamically important and resistive effects are present.

how_they_decided_enough.value: Included all cores with at least 20 polarization semi-vectors above 3 sigma_P after Monte Carlo subsampling tests on cores #1 and #14 showed that reducing from 45 to 20 semi-vectors changes angle dispersion by at most 10%.

evidence.quote: To maximize the number of cores for which a magnetic field strength can be derived, we included all cores containing at least 20 semi-vectors.
As shown in Appendix 7, the resulting angle dispersion varies by 10 % at most, demonstrating that the magnetic field strength estimate is robust against moderate incompleteness in the sampling.

limitations_admitted.value: Core linewidths cannot disentangle micro-turbulence from organized motions (infall, rotation, converging flows) at the core scale because the beam size is comparable to the core size.

evidence.quote: We will refer this as the turbulence level but we put forward that, within the cores, we cannot disentangle turbulence from other types of gas motion.

evidence.loc: Velocity structures in the three-beam area
evidence.quote: Given that the beam size is comparable to the core size, the observed velocity field mainly reflects averaged motions at this scale, while potential sub-beam velocity structures would remain unresolved.

limitations_admitted.value: Using different molecular tracers (DCN, 13CS, CH3CN) may introduce small systematic differences in linewidth because they trace different gas layers.

evidence.quote: The use of different tracers may introduce small systematic differences in linewidth values as they do not necessarily trace the same gas, but it is essential in order to make a statistical study of cores.

limitations_admitted.value: Cores #3, #4, #5, and #9 have polarization angle dispersions sigma_theta > 25 deg, exceeding the regime where the classical DCF method is strictly reliable.

evidence.quote: As explained in Sect. 4.1, the DCF method is reliable for regions with $\sigma_\theta < 25^{\circ}$, which here is the case for all the cores except cores #3, #4, #5 and #9 that we decided to keep in the following analysis in order to preserve the statistical significance of the sample.

limitations_admitted.value: Mass-to-flux ratios lambda_B only account for the plane-of-sky magnetic field (representing a lower limit to the 3D ratio) and suffer from projection/simulation biases noted by Tritsis et al. (2026).

evidence.loc: Magnetic support and its relative contribution
evidence.quote: It is important to note that this mass-to-flux ratio, which only accounts for the plane-of-sky magnetic field, represents a lower limit to the true mass-to-flux ratio that includes the full three-dimensional magnetic field.

evidence.loc: Magnetic support and its relative contribution
evidence.quote: We also note that, as pointed out by (cite: Tritsis2026), mass-to-flux ratio estimates derived from $B_{\mathrm{POS}}$ are subject to significant limitations.

limitations_admitted.value: The simplified virial analysis neglects surface terms (confining thermal, kinetic, and magnetic pressure) and central protostellar masses, and depends on assumed temperature, geometry, and density profile index p.

evidence.quote: We note that, for protostellar cores, the mass of the central protostar is not included in the total mass, as reliable measurements are not available.

evidence.loc: Limitations of current observational estimates of the non-thermal supports
evidence.quote: The surface terms (such as the confining pressure exerted by the surrounding medium) are extremely difficult to be constrained observationally and are therefore not included here, even though they would further reduce the effective values of $\alpha_{\mathrm{vir,B}}$.

referee_caveats_inferred: Extrapolating B_POS from the ~12,500 au three-beam scale down to ~2,500 au core scales using a literature Zeeman power-law (B proportional to n^0.53) assumes a smooth, universal scaling across a dynamical region where 3 cores (#4, #10, #146) actually have higher surrounding density than core density.

In Table 1 vs Section 5.4 text, core #6's alpha_kin is listed as 0.32 in Table 1 but cited as 0.55 in the text of Section 5.4, indicating a minor internal inconsistency (likely due to p=0 vs p=2 or an earlier catalog mass).

The two most massive hot cores (#1 and #4) rely on CH3CN(5_3-4_3) at 1.6 km s^-1 spectral resolution without an empirical scaling factor to DCN, which may systematically affect the high-mass end of the kinetic support distribution.

reproducibility.score_reason: All four ALMA project codes, target coordinates, line frequencies, equations, and per-core intermediate and final measurements (Table 1 and Table B.1) are explicitly provided, though full end-to-end reproduction requires external ALMA-IMF catalog tables (Nony et al. 2023; Motte et al. 2025) and inherited imaging parameters (Cunningham et al. 2023; Arce-Tord et al. 2020).
